newsitem.title: USA: Large grain imports by Russia not seen soon - trade.
newsitem.headline: Large grain imports by Russia not seen soon - trade.

text.p: No large-scale imports of grain by Russia are seen in the next five years as government purchases of grain decline and private traders build their fledgling businesses, a Russian grain trader said Wednesday.
"It will be quite a long time, and it (Russian imports) will mostly be feedgrains, not wheat," said Arkady Zlochevsky, chairman of OGO Firm, who spoke through a translator.
Zlochevsky and other private grain traders from Russia were in the U.S. to learn how grain companies and commodity exchanges here work. Their trip was sponsored by the U.S. Feed Grains Council.

Current export sales data supports Russia's increased demand for corn. According to last week's export sales report from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, U.S. exporters sold 42,000 tonnes of corn to Russia, versus 10,500 during the same period last year.
Last week's wheat sales were 45,000 tonnes, verus year-ago sales of 130,300, USDA said.
Zlochevsky and other Russian traders said the bulk of grain trade between the U.S. and Russia is now composed of small private deals rather than the large government trades known in the 1980s.
"All of that is in the past," said Alexander Kholopov, USFGC representative in Moscow. "The private companies have the money and can pay cash."
Private companies will also be less likely to enter into barter deals because they have money, the traders said.
Government purchases to maintain Russian stockpiles of grain will be made "on a very limited level," Kholopov said.
For example, a private firm just purchased 35,000 tonnes of corn last week, while the last government-financed purchase of U.S. totaled only 11,000 tonnes, USFG representatives said.
In its March supply and demand report, the U.S. Department of Agriculture forecast Russian corn imports for 1996-97 at 200,000 tonnes and wheat imports at 2.5 million.
There have been some market rumors that the Russian government was planning a large wheat purchase in the near-term, but the Russian traders were quick to dismiss the talk.
"In the domestic markets, there are elevators holding wheat they can't sell," Zlochevsky said.
Any government wheat purchases will be made only for residents of far eastern Russia, where supplies are scant, he said.
Weather had not been favorable for the Russian grain crop for the past several years and this year was no exception, Zlochevsky said.
He would not, however estimate 1997 Russian net grain production. Earlier this year, Russia's Agriculture Ministry forecast net grain production at 70.0 million tonnes, up from 69.3 in 1996.
The largest problem facing Russian farmers is the country's poor soil health and a widespread lack of fertilizer and other inputs, the grain dealers said.
"It's difficult to get the fertility of the soil back," Zlochevsky said. "The soil becomes salty and becomes degraded."
